body:
Why land revenue was important to the East India Company

Land revenue was one of the principal sources of income for the British administration in India. Since agriculture supported a large proportion of the population, the government could obtain substantial income by taxing agricultural land and its produce.

On 12 August 1765, the Mughal emperor granted the East India Company the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Diwani meant the authority to administer and collect revenue. The Company, which had originally entered India as a trading organisation, now became responsible for managing the financial resources of these territories.

Revenue collected in India helped the Company finance its administration, military expenses and purchases of Indian goods for export. The Company therefore wanted a system that could provide a regular and substantial income.

However, excessive revenue demands contributed to difficulties in the countryside. Cultivators struggled to pay their dues, agricultural production suffered, and the Bengal economy experienced a serious crisis. The devastating Bengal famine of 1770 further demonstrated the vulnerability of the rural economy.

Meaning of land revenue settlement

A land revenue settlement was an arrangement through which the colonial government determined the amount of revenue payable from agricultural land, identified who was responsible for payment and established the period for which the assessment would remain valid.

A settlement was not merely a method of collecting money. It also influenced the rights and responsibilities of cultivators, landlords and village communities.

Important terms

  • Land revenue: The payment demanded by the government from agricultural land or those liable to pay it.
  • Rent: A payment made by a tenant or cultivator to a landlord or another person holding rights over the land. Rent received by a landlord was not necessarily equal to the revenue payable to the government.
  • Ryot or raiyat: A peasant or cultivator. A ryot might cultivate land personally or, in some situations, allow another person to cultivate part of the holding.
  • Zamindar: A person possessing recognised rights or authority over an estate and, under the Permanent Settlement, responsible for collecting rent and paying a specified revenue demand to the government.
  • Assessment: The process of determining the revenue demand, often using information about land area, soil quality, cultivation and estimated agricultural production.
  • Intermediary: A person or institution standing between the cultivator and the government in the collection of land revenue.

Why different systems developed

British officials did not introduce one uniform land revenue system throughout India. They adopted different arrangements according to their understanding of existing landholding practices, village institutions and the government's financial requirements.

The 3 principal systems were the Permanent Settlement, the Ryotwari Settlement and the Mahalwari Settlement.

Their most important differences concerned the person or institution responsible for government revenue, the role of intermediaries and whether the government's assessment could be revised.

The distinction between permanent and temporary settlements

Under a permanent settlement, the government's assessed revenue demand was fixed without a scheduled future revision. Under a temporary settlement, the assessment remained valid for a specified period and could subsequently be revised.

The word temporary did not mean that revenue was collected only briefly. It meant that the assessment was not fixed for all future time.

The government revenue demand, the rent collected from cultivators and the rights of the people occupying the land were separate matters. Fixing one did not automatically fix the others.

Prelims focus

  • 1765: The Company obtained Diwani rights in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
  • Permanent Settlement: The zamindar became the principal revenue-paying intermediary.
  • Ryotwari: The individual cultivator was directly responsible for government revenue.
  • Mahalwari: The village or revenue estate formed the principal settlement unit.
  • Trap: A permanent government revenue demand did not mean permanently fixed rents for all cultivators.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8 History, Chapter 3, Ruling the Countryside, printed pp. 26–30, 2020–21 textbook edition in GPSC Volume 04; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Theme 9, Colonialism and the Countryside, printed pp. 228–229, online 2024–25 edition consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Land Revenue under British Rule: Background, Purpose and Basic Concepts

body:
Introduction of the Permanent Settlement

The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 under Lord Cornwallis, who was then the Governor-General of Bengal. It became particularly associated with Bengal and Bihar and was also applied in certain other eastern territories under British administration.

The arrangement is commonly called the Zamindari Settlement because zamindars became the principal intermediaries between the government and the cultivators.

The Company recognised existing rajas and taluqdars as zamindars for the purposes of revenue administration. They became responsible for collecting rent from cultivators and paying the government a specified amount of revenue.

How the system operated

Under the Permanent Settlement, the colonial government fixed the total revenue demand payable by a zamindar from the estate. This amount was to remain unchanged in perpetuity.

The zamindar collected rent from the peasants occupying or cultivating land in the estate. After paying the required government revenue, the zamindar retained the remaining income, subject to the costs and obligations of managing the estate.

The meaning of permanence

The most distinctive provision was that the government's assessed revenue demand was fixed permanently. If agricultural production increased or produce prices rose, the government could not simply increase that existing permanently settled demand.

However, the rents collected by zamindars from their tenants were not permanently fixed by the settlement. Consequently, increases in agricultural income could benefit zamindars without producing a corresponding increase in the Company's permanently settled revenue.

Permanent Settlement fixed the government's claim against the zamindar, not the rent of every cultivator. It also did not guarantee that a zamindar could retain an estate after failing to pay the government's demand.

Rights of zamindars and cultivators

Position of zamindars

The settlement strengthened the recognised estate-level rights of zamindars. They were treated as proprietors for important purposes of colonial land administration and could derive income from the land under their control.

Nevertheless, a zamindar did not necessarily cultivate the land personally or own every individual field in the ordinary sense. The zamindari was also a revenue estate: the zamindar had contracted to pay the government's assessed demand and remained subject to its enforcement.

Zamindars could hold extensive estates containing several villages. Their principal obligation to the Company was to pay the required revenue at the prescribed time.

Position of cultivators

The ryots continued to cultivate the land, but many had limited security against the demands of zamindars. The settlement did not itself guarantee a permanently fixed rent or uniform, secure occupancy rights for every tenant.

Cultivators could face increased rents, indebtedness or eviction, particularly when they were unable to satisfy the landlord's demands. The actual position varied with local customs, tenant rights and subsequent legal developments.

Why British officials introduced the system

The Permanent Settlement was expected to serve 2 principal purposes.

  • Regular government revenue: A known annual demand would provide the Company with a predictable income.
  • Encouragement of agricultural improvement: Officials expected zamindars to invest in land because they could retain the increased income produced by improvements without facing an increase in the government's permanently fixed demand.

The government hoped that secure estate rights and the possibility of greater profits would encourage the expansion of cultivation and investment in agricultural production.

Payment obligation and loss of estates

The permanently fixed amount had to be paid on time. A zamindar who failed to meet the government's demand could lose the estate through a revenue auction.

Therefore, permanence referred to the assessed amount, not an unconditional right to retain the estate.

The arrangement could provide an incentive to improve agriculture, but it could also encourage zamindars to increase collections from tenants. Whether the expected investment occurred depended on conditions such as the size of the government demand, agricultural prices and the zamindar's ability to collect rent.

Prelims focus

  • 1793: Introduction of the Permanent Settlement.
  • Lord Cornwallis: Governor-General associated with its introduction.
  • Main intermediary: Zamindar.
  • Principal regions: Bengal and Bihar, with application in certain other eastern territories.
  • Government revenue: Fixed in perpetuity.
  • Trap: Zamindars could lose their estates through revenue auctions despite the settlement being permanent.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8 History, Chapter 3, Ruling the Countryside, printed pp. 28–29, 2020–21 edition in GPSC Volume 04; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Theme 9, sections 1.1–1.3, printed pp. 228–230, online 2024–25 edition consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Permanent Settlement of 1793: Features, Rights and Revenue Collection

body:
Why zamindars faced difficulties

The Permanent Settlement was intended to encourage agricultural investment and provide the Company with reliable revenue. Its early operation, however, revealed important difficulties.

The government's initial revenue demand was fixed at a high level. Officials anticipated that agricultural production and prices might increase in the future. Because the demand would remain unchanged, they sought to secure a substantial amount from the beginning.

This high assessment created difficulties when agricultural prices were low or harvests were poor. Cultivators could not always pay the rent demanded by zamindars, and zamindars consequently struggled to meet their fixed obligations to the Company.

Why a permanently fixed demand could lead to auctions

The obligation to pay government revenue did not automatically decrease when a crop failed. The zamindar remained responsible for the assessed amount even when rent collection was difficult.

Revenue payments also had to be made by specified deadlines. Under the provision commonly known as the Sunset Law, failure to make the required payment by sunset on the appointed date could make the zamindari liable to auction.

Numerous zamindaris were sold because their holders failed to pay the government revenue. Such auctions could transfer estate rights to new purchasers.

1797, Burdwan, Bengal: Estates belonging to the Raja of Burdwan were put up for auction because of accumulated revenue arrears. The case illustrates the enforcement of the Permanent Settlement's payment obligations.

The Burdwan auction also showed that an official sale did not always result in an effective transfer of local control. Some purchases were arranged through agents acting for the previous estate holder.

What happened when agricultural prices increased

From the early 19th century, agricultural prices began to rise and cultivation gradually expanded in Bengal.

Zamindars who could collect greater rents had an opportunity to increase their income. The Company's existing revenue demand, however, remained fixed.

This produced an important difference between the interests of the government and those of the zamindars. Increased agricultural income could raise the earnings of estate holders without increasing the revenue payable to the Company.

Why the expected agricultural improvements were limited

The expectation that zamindars would invest heavily in agricultural improvement was not generally fulfilled.

Initially, the high revenue demand made many zamindars financially insecure. Some lost their estates through auctions, while others could not easily accumulate resources for investment.

Later, when cultivation expanded and prices increased, zamindars could often obtain additional income by collecting rent rather than investing in improvements to the land.

Thus, a system designed to encourage agricultural development did not necessarily produce the intended investment.

Effects on cultivators

Many cultivators experienced high rent demands and insecure rights over their holdings. When they could not pay, they might have to borrow from moneylenders. Continued indebtedness could make their economic position increasingly difficult.

Some cultivators also faced eviction from land that their families had cultivated for generations.

The situation was not identical for every cultivator or estate. More prosperous peasants and local holders of land could possess greater bargaining power, while poorer tenants and under-tenants were generally more vulnerable.

Overall assessment

The Permanent Settlement created a lasting distinction between the government's fixed demand and the income obtainable by zamindars from cultivation.

It encouraged the growth of an estate-based landlord class but did not guarantee improved agricultural production or secure conditions for cultivators.

Its limitations also influenced subsequent British policy. In newly acquired territories during the 19th century, officials increasingly preferred settlements under which the government's revenue demand could be reassessed periodically.

Prelims focus

  • High initial assessment: An important cause of early zamindari defaults.
  • Sunset Law: Failure to meet the prescribed payment deadline could lead to an estate auction.
  • 1797: Revenue auction involving the Burdwan estate.
  • After 1810: Rising agricultural prices increased opportunities for zamindari income.
  • Government revenue: The permanently settled demand could not be raised merely because agricultural income increased.
  • Trap: The expectation of agricultural investment should not be confused with evidence that zamindars generally made such investments.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8 History, Chapter 3, Ruling the Countryside, printed pp. 28–29, 2020–21 edition in GPSC Volume 04; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Theme 9, sections 1.1–1.4 and 3.2, printed pp. 228–231 and 247–248, online 2024–25 edition consulted 20 November 2026.]
